exp_1_1_titel: How do you make a bulb light up?
exp_1_1_frage: In front of you are a battery, a bulb and some wires. Is one single wire from the battery to the bulb enough to make it light up?
exp_1_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp_1_1_s1: Drag a bulb from the parts tray onto fields A1 and A2.
exp_1_1_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to A1. Switch on the main switch. Does the bulb light up?
exp_1_1_s3: Now draw a black wire from A2 to 0V. What happens?
exp_1_1_h1: The current needs a way there and a way back.
exp_1_1_h2: Both ends of the bulb must be connected to the battery.
exp_1_1_loesung: One wire from +9V to A1, a second one from A2 to 0V – and switch on the main switch.
exp_1_1_erklaerung: Current only flows in a loop: from the battery through the bulb and back to the battery. If part of the path is missing, the loop is open and nothing lights up. That is why it is called an electric circuit.
exp_1_1_mehr: Here the battery is set to 4.5 V. The bulb is made for 6 V, so it glows a little dimmer. A bulb lights up because its very thin wire gets very hot.
exp_1_1_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. How bright is the bulb now?
exp_1_1_w2: Swap the two wires at the bulb. Does it still light up?
exp_1_1_echt: With a flat battery (4.5 V), a bulb from the craft shop and two wires, you can build this circuit for real.
exp_1_2_frage: A doorbell only rings while someone presses the button. Where does the push button have to go so that your buzzer works the same way?
exp_1_2_v1: The push button belongs in the path of the current to the buzzer.
exp_1_2_v2: The push button can be anywhere next to it.
exp_1_2_s1: Put the push button on fields A2 and A3.
exp_1_2_s2: Put the buzzer on A3 and A4. Its plus leg goes to A3.
exp_1_2_s3: Draw a red wire from +9V to A2 and a black one from A4 to 0V. Switch on and press the button!
exp_1_2_h1: A push button is a bridge that only holds while you press it.
exp_1_2_h2: The push button and the buzzer must be one after the other in the same circuit.
exp_1_2_loesung: +9V to A2, push button from A2 to A3, buzzer from A3 to A4 (plus at A3), A4 to 0V. Main switch on, then hold the push button down.
exp_1_2_erklaerung: The push button interrupts the circuit. When you press it, it closes the gap: current flows through the buzzer and it buzzes. When you let go, the circuit is open again. Parts placed one after the other like this form a series circuit.
exp_1_2_mehr: Inside your buzzer, a thin plate vibrates about 2400 times every second. You hear it as a high tone.
exp_1_2_w1: Put the push button somewhere else in the circuit, for example between the buzzer and 0V. Does it still ring?
exp_1_2_echt: With a 4.5 V battery, a buzzer and a push button, you can build a doorbell for your bedroom door.
exp_1_3_titel: The panel switch makes the motor run
exp_1_3_frage: A push button only holds while you press it. A switch stays the way you set it. Which is better if a fan should run for a long time?
exp_1_3_v1: The switch, because it stays on.
exp_1_3_v2: The push button, because it is easier to press.
exp_1_3_s1: Put the motor on fields C1 and C3.
exp_1_3_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to the panel field S1 and a second one from S2 to C1.
exp_1_3_s3: Draw a black wire from C3 to 0V. Switch on the main switch and then the panel switch S.
exp_1_3_h1: The panel switch S has two fields: S1 and S2. The current has to pass through it.
exp_1_3_h2: The path of the current: +9V, switch S, motor, 0V.
exp_1_3_loesung: +9V to S1, S2 to C1, motor from C1 to C3, C3 to 0V. Then switch on the main switch and the panel switch S.
exp_1_3_erklaerung: A switch keeps the circuit closed until you flip it back. So the motor runs without you having to press all the time. The main switch of the battery is also a switch like this.
exp_1_3_mehr: A motor turns electric current into a turning movement. The higher the voltage, the faster it turns.
exp_1_3_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V and then to 3 V. How does the motor change?
exp_1_3_w2: Swap the wires at C1 and C3. Which way does the motor turn now?
exp_1_3_echt: Many toys have small motors with a switch and batteries inside. Look where the switch is.
exp_2_4_titel: Why does the LED need a protector?
exp_2_4_frage: So far you have connected bulbs directly to the battery. Today you try an LED. It is much smaller and needs less current. Can you connect it just like a bulb?
exp_2_4_v1: Yes, it lights up the same way.
exp_2_4_v2: It shines brighter than the bulb.
exp_2_4_s1: Put the LED from B4 to C4. The long leg goes to B4. Draw a red wire from +9V to B4 and a black one from C4 to 0V. Switch on!
exp_2_4_s2: Repair the LED with a tap. Put the resistor with the rings yellow, violet, brown from B3 to B4. Move the end of the red wire from B4 to B3. What happens now?
exp_2_4_h1: Think: what slows down the current when there is no bulb in the circuit?
exp_2_4_h2: Look at fields B3 and B4. Something is still missing there.
exp_2_4_loesung: The resistor goes between +9V and the LED: from B3 to B4.
exp_2_4_erklaerung: A bulb slows the current down by itself, because its thin wire makes the way hard. The LED hardly does that. Without a brake, so much current flows that it gets too hot. The resistor is its protector: it only lets through as much current as the LED can take.
exp_2_4_mehr: With 470 ohms, about (9 V − 1.9 V) / 470 Ω ≈ 15 mA flows. The LED can take 20 mA continuously.
exp_2_4_w1: Replace the resistor with one of 1 kΩ. Does the LED get brighter or darker?
exp_2_4_echt: Build the circuit with your experiment kit – but only with the resistor! A real LED cannot be repaired with a tap.
lex_gluehlampe: A bulb lights up because a very thin wire gets very hot.
lex_taster: A push button only closes the circuit while you press it.
lex_wechselschalter: A changeover switch connects its middle either to one terminal or to the other. That way you can switch a light from two places.
lex_reedkontakt: A reed switch is a switch inside a small glass tube. If you hold a magnet next to it, it closes.
lex_motor: A motor turns electric current into a turning movement.
lex_summer: A buzzer hums or beeps when current flows through it.
lex_widerstand: A resistor slows down the current. The colour rings tell you how much.
lex_led: An LED only lights up in one direction and always needs a series resistor.
lex_diode: A diode only lets current through in one direction – like a one-way street.
lex_kondensator: A capacitor stores electric charge for a short time.
lex_elko: An electrolytic capacitor has a plus and a minus pole. Plugged in the wrong way round, it breaks.
lex_fotowiderstand: A photoresistor lets more current through in light than in the dark.
lex_transistor: A transistor is a switch controlled by a small current. It sits on a small board with four feet: B and C at the top, E twice at the bottom – the two E feet are connected on the board.
lex_blinkmodul: The blinker module switches its output on and off again and again.
lex_tonmodul: The tone module makes a sound as long as its input gets current.
stufe_0_frage: How do I make something blink?
stufe_1_frage: When does the bulb light up?
stufe_2_frage: What happens if I add a second bulb?
stufe_3_frage: How much current is actually flowing?
stufe_4_frage: How can one current control another?
exp_1_1_b1: With one wire the bulb stayed dark; with two wires it lit up.
exp_1_1_b2: The bulb already lit up with one wire.
exp_1_2_b1: The buzzer only buzzed while I was pressing the button.
exp_1_2_b2: The buzzer buzzed all the time.
exp_1_3_b1: The motor kept running without me holding anything down.
exp_2_4_b1: Without a resistor the LED broke; with the resistor it lit up.
exp_2_4_b2: The LED lit up normally without a resistor.
exp_2_4_b3: The LED did not light up at all.
exp_0_1_frage: There is a blinker module in the module bar at the bottom. Do you think you can make a light blink in just a few steps?
exp_0_1_b2: The LED stays on all the time.
exp_0_1_b3: It blinks, but I don't know why.
exp_0_1_s1: Put the resistor from B3 to B4 and the red LED from B4 to C4 (long leg to B4).
exp_0_1_s2: Connect +9V to the plus of the blinker module (M1) and minus (M2) to 0V.
exp_0_1_s3: Draw a wire from +9V to B3 and one from C4 to the module output (M3). Switch on!
exp_0_1_h1: The module needs power itself: plus and minus must go to the battery.
exp_0_1_h2: The module output switches the LED's path to 0V on and off.
exp_0_1_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, C4 → M3. Main switch on.
exp_0_1_erklaerung: The blinker module is a little switch that keeps turning itself on and off. You'll find out later how it works – at the end of the learning path you'll even build such a blinker from single parts.
exp_0_1_mehr: The module switches about once per second.
exp_0_1_w1: Use a green LED instead of the red one. Does it blink the same way?
exp_0_1_echt: You can find blinking lights on bike lamps, building sites and smoke detectors. On your next walk, look out for everything that blinks.
exp_1_4_frage: A torch only lights up when you press the button. What do you need besides a battery and a bulb?
exp_1_4_v1: A push button in the circuit.
exp_1_4_b1: The bulb only lights while I press the button.
exp_1_4_b2: The bulb lights all the time.
exp_1_4_s1: Put the push button on A2 and A3 and the bulb on A3 and A4.
exp_1_4_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to A2 and a black one from A4 to 0V.
exp_1_4_s3: Switch on and press the button.
exp_1_4_h1: The button must be able to interrupt the current's path to the bulb.
exp_1_4_h2: Button and bulb lie one after the other between +9V and 0V.
exp_1_4_loesung: +9V → A2, button A2–A3, bulb A3–A4, A4 → 0V. Main switch on, press the button.
exp_1_4_erklaerung: The button is a gap in the circuit that you close with your finger. That's exactly how a torch button works.
exp_1_4_mehr: Many torches have a switch that stays on instead of a push button.
exp_1_4_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. How bright is your torch now?
exp_1_4_echt: Open up an old torch with an adult: can you find the battery, bulb and switch?
exp_1_5_frage: This bulb is made for 2.5 V. The battery is set to 3 V. Do they go together?
exp_1_5_v1: Yes, 3 V is close enough to 2.5 V.
exp_1_5_b1: The bulb shines brightly and stays intact.
exp_1_5_s1: Put a bulb on B2 and B3. Choose the rated voltage 2.5 V in the part menu.
exp_1_5_s2: Draw a wire from +9V to B2 and from B3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_1_5_h1: The rated voltage is shown at the bulb. A long press or right-click opens the menu.
exp_1_5_loesung: Bulb B2–B3 at 2.5 V, +9V → B2, B3 → 0V, battery 3 V, main switch on.
exp_1_5_erklaerung: A bulb can take a little more than its rated voltage, but not much more. 3 V on a 2.5 V bulb just makes it a bit brighter. Far too much voltage would burn through the thin wire.
exp_1_5_mehr: The rated voltage is the voltage a part is made for.
exp_1_5_w1: Use a 6 V bulb at 3 V. How bright is it?
exp_1_5_echt: Real bulbs have the voltage printed on them. Read it before you connect a bulb to a battery.
exp_1_6_titel: A fan at the push of a button
exp_1_6_frage: You want a little fan that only turns while you press. How do you build it?
exp_1_6_v1: With a push button in front of the motor.
exp_1_6_b1: The motor only turns while I press.
exp_1_6_b2: The motor turns all the time.
exp_1_6_s1: Put the button on A1 and A2 and the motor from A2 to A4.
exp_1_6_s2: Draw a wire from +9V to A1 and a black one from A4 to 0V. Switch on and press.
exp_1_6_h1: The motor is long: it needs two fields of distance.
exp_1_6_h2: Button and motor lie one after the other.
exp_1_6_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, motor A2–A4, A4 → 0V. Main switch on, press the button.
exp_1_6_erklaerung: Current can make not only light but also movement. The motor turns the current into rotation – but only as long as the button closes the circuit.
exp_1_6_mehr: Light, heat, movement and sound are the effects of current you experience in Volta.
exp_1_6_w1: Swap the two wires at the motor. Does it turn the other way now?
exp_1_6_echt: Small motors with buttons are in toy cars and mixers. Ask an adult whether you can look at one together.
exp_1_7_frage: In your room the light stays on when you flip the switch. Can the panel switch S do that with a bulb?
exp_1_7_v2: No, I have to press all the time.
exp_1_7_b1: The bulb stays on until I switch S off again.
exp_1_7_b2: The bulb goes out straight away.
exp_1_7_s1: Put a bulb on B1 and B2.
exp_1_7_s2: Draw wires: +9V to S1, S2 to B1, B2 to 0V.
exp_1_7_s3: Switch on the main switch and then S.
exp_1_7_h1: S1 and S2 are the two terminals of the panel switch.
exp_1_7_h2: The current flows: +9V, switch S, bulb, 0V.
exp_1_7_loesung: +9V → S1, S2 → B1, bulb B1–B2, B2 → 0V; main switch and S on.
exp_1_7_erklaerung: A switch remembers its position. That's why the light stays on until you turn it off – just like the light switch in your room.
exp_1_7_mehr: Push button: only while you press. Switch: stays the way you set it.
exp_1_7_w1: Replace the bulb with the buzzer. What changes?
exp_1_7_echt: At home, count how many switches and how many push buttons (like the doorbell) you can find.
exp_2_1_titel: Two bulbs one after the other
exp_2_1_frage: What happens if you connect two bulbs one after the other to the battery?
exp_2_1_v1: Both shine as brightly as one alone.
exp_2_1_b1: Both light up, but each dimmer than alone.
exp_2_1_s1: Put one bulb on A1–A2 and a second one on A2–A3.
exp_2_1_s2: Draw wires from +9V to A1 and from A3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_1_h1: The current flows through one bulb first, then the other.
exp_2_1_loesung: +9V → A1, bulb A1–A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V, battery 9 V.
exp_2_1_erklaerung: One after the other, the bulbs share the battery's voltage: each gets only half. That's why both are dimmer. This is called a series circuit.
exp_2_1_mehr: At 9 V each of the two 6 V bulbs gets about 4.5 V.
exp_2_1_w1: Turn on the voltage display at A2. How many bars do you see?
exp_2_1_w2: Take one bulb out. What happens to the other one?
exp_2_1_echt: Old fairy lights were series circuits: if one bulb broke, the whole string went dark.
exp_2_2_frage: This time each bulb gets its own path to the battery. Do they shine brighter than in a row?
exp_2_2_s1: Put one bulb on A1–A2 and one on B1–B2.
exp_2_2_s2: Connect A1 to B1 and A2 to B2.
exp_2_2_s3: Draw +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_2_h1: Each bulb should be connected directly to the battery at both ends.
exp_2_2_h2: Two cross wires connect the bulbs: A1–B1 and A2–B2.
exp_2_2_loesung: Bulbs A1–A2 and B1–B2, wires A1–B1, A2–B2, +9V → A1, A2 → 0V, battery 4.5 V.
exp_2_2_erklaerung: Side by side, each bulb gets the battery's full voltage. That's why both shine brightly. The battery has to deliver more current for it. This is called a parallel circuit.
exp_2_2_mehr: At home all lamps are connected in parallel – that's why each shines equally, however many are on.
exp_2_2_w1: Take one bulb out. Does the other keep shining?
exp_2_2_echt: Modern fairy lights are often wired in parallel. If one light fails, the others keep shining.
exp_2_3_frage: A machine should only run if panel switch S is on AND someone presses the button. How do you connect switch and button?
exp_2_3_b1: The bulb only lights when S is on and I press.
exp_2_3_s1: Put the button on A1–A2 and the bulb on A2–A3.
exp_2_3_s2: Draw +9V to S1, S2 to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp_2_3_s3: Try all four possibilities: S on/off, button pressed/not pressed.
exp_2_3_h1: The current should go through S first and then through the button.
exp_2_3_h2: If either is missing, the circuit is open.
exp_2_3_loesung: +9V → S1, S2 → A1, button A1–A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V. S on, press the button.
exp_2_3_erklaerung: When two switches lie one after the other, the current must pass through both. The bulb only lights if the first AND the second are closed. That's an AND circuit.
exp_2_3_mehr: Big machines have such safety features: they only run if two buttons are pressed at the same time.
exp_2_3_w1: Make a table: when does the bulb light and when not?
exp_2_3_echt: Some washing machines only start if the door is closed AND you press start.
exp_2_5_frage: A light should come on if panel switch S is on OR the button is pressed. How do you connect the two?
exp_2_5_b1: The bulb lights as soon as either one is closed.
exp_2_5_s1: Put the button on A1–A2 and the bulb on A2–A3.
exp_2_5_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and also +9V to S1, then S2 to A2.
exp_2_5_s3: Draw A3 to 0V. Try button and S one at a time.
exp_2_5_h1: The current should have two paths to the bulb.
exp_2_5_h2: S bridges the button: S1 to +9V, S2 to A2.
exp_2_5_loesung: +9V → A1 and +9V → S1, button A1–A2, S2 → A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V.
exp_2_5_erklaerung: When two switches lie side by side, the current has two paths. One open path is enough: the bulb lights if one OR the other is closed. That's an OR circuit.
exp_2_5_mehr: A car's interior light comes on if one OR the other door is open.
exp_2_5_w1: Compare with the AND circuit: what is wired differently?
exp_2_5_echt: A doorbell with two buttons, at the front and back of the house, is an OR circuit.
exp_2_6_frage: On a staircase you can switch the light on downstairs and off upstairs. How does that work with two switches?
exp_2_6_v1: With two changeover switches and two wires between them.
exp_2_6_v2: With two normal switches one after the other.
exp_2_6_b1: Each changeover switch can toggle the light, whatever the other's position.
exp_2_6_s1: Put one changeover switch on A1–A3, another on C1–C3 and the bulb on C5–C6.
exp_2_6_s2: Connect A1 to C1 and A3 to C3.
exp_2_6_s3: Draw +9V to A2, C2 to C5 and C6 to 0V. Tap the switches.
exp_2_6_h1: The middle of a changeover switch connects either to A or to B.
exp_2_6_h2: Two wires run between the switches: A to A and B to B.
exp_2_6_loesung: W1 on A1–A3, W2 on C1–C3, A1 → C1, A3 → C3, +9V → A2, C2 → C5, bulb C5–C6, C6 → 0V.
exp_2_6_erklaerung: The light is on when both changeover switches point to the same wire. If you flip one, they point to different wires and the path is broken. That way each switch can toggle the light.
exp_2_6_mehr: This circuit is called a two-way switching circuit. It's in almost every staircase and long hallway.
exp_2_6_w1: Try all four positions and note when the light is on.
exp_2_6_echt: Find a hallway at home or at school where you can switch the light at both ends.
exp_2_7_frage: A diode only lets current through in one direction. Does a bulb light if a diode sits in front of it?
exp_2_7_v1: Yes, if the diode is the right way round.
exp_2_7_b1: The right way round the bulb lights; the wrong way it stays dark.
exp_2_7_s1: Put the diode from B2 to B3 (ring towards B3) and a 10 V bulb on B3–B4.
exp_2_7_s2: Draw +9V to B2 and B4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_7_s3: Flip the diode (part menu: Flip). What happens?
exp_2_7_h1: The ring on the diode shows where the current may flow.
exp_2_7_h2: The ring belongs to the side that leads to 0V.
exp_2_7_loesung: +9V → B2, diode B2–B3 (ring at B3), 10 V bulb B3–B4, B4 → 0V.
exp_2_7_erklaerung: The diode is like a one-way street for current. In the forward direction it lets it through; in the reverse direction it stops it. That's why it matters which way round you put it.
exp_2_7_mehr: A diode uses up about 0.7 V. That's why you use a 10 V bulb here: it gets about 8.3 V.
exp_2_7_w1: Turn on the voltage display at B3 and flip the diode. What changes?
exp_2_7_echt: Diodes protect many devices: if you put the battery in the wrong way round, no current flows and nothing breaks.
exp_2_8_frage: An LED has a long and a short leg. Does it also light if you put it in the other way round?
exp_2_8_v1: No, only the right way round.
exp_2_8_b1: The other way round it stayed dark; the right way round it lights.
exp_2_8_s1: Put the resistor on B3–B4 and the LED from B4 to C4.
exp_2_8_s2: Draw +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_8_s3: Flip the LED until it lights.
exp_2_8_h1: An LED is a diode that lights – so it's a one-way street too.
exp_2_8_h2: The long leg (anode) belongs on the +9V side.
exp_2_8_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED long leg at B4, short leg at C4, C4 → 0V.
exp_2_8_erklaerung: An LED only lights in the forward direction. The long leg (anode) must go to plus, the short one (cathode) to minus. The wrong way round no current flows – but it doesn't break.
exp_2_8_mehr: The cathode side of the housing is often flattened.
exp_2_8_w1: Take a blue LED. Does it light with the same resistor?
exp_2_8_echt: Look at a real LED with an adult: can you find the long and the short leg?
exp_2_9_frage: A reed switch closes when a magnet is nearby. Can you build an alarm that buzzes when the magnet comes?
exp_2_9_v1: Yes, reed switch and buzzer one after the other.
exp_2_9_v2: I need a push button for that.
exp_2_9_b1: With the magnet it buzzes, without it it's quiet.
exp_2_9_s1: Put the reed switch on A1–A2 and the buzzer on A2–A3 (plus at A2).
exp_2_9_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_9_s3: Tap the reed switch – that holds the magnet next to it.
exp_2_9_h1: The reed switch is a switch operated by the magnet.
exp_2_9_h2: Reed switch and buzzer lie one after the other between +9V and 0V.
exp_2_9_loesung: +9V → A1, reed switch A1–A2, buzzer A2–A3, A3 → 0V. Bring the magnet close (tap).
exp_2_9_erklaerung: Inside the reed switch's glass tube are two thin metal tongues. A magnet pulls them together and the circuit closes. That's how a window or door can trigger an alarm.
exp_2_9_mehr: In real alarms the reed switch sits in the frame and the magnet in the window.
exp_2_9_w1: Build the alarm with a bulb instead of the buzzer. Which is easier to notice?
exp_2_9_echt: Some bike computers count wheel turns with a reed switch and a magnet on a spoke.
exp_2_10_frage: The blinker module switches on and off in rhythm. What happens if you connect the buzzer instead of a light?
exp_2_10_v2: The buzzer buzzes without a break.
exp_2_10_b1: The buzzer beeps briefly again and again.
exp_2_10_b2: The buzzer buzzes without a break.
exp_2_10_s1: Connect the blinker module: +9V to M1, M2 to 0V.
exp_2_10_s2: Put the buzzer on B2–B3 (plus at B2), draw +9V to B2.
exp_2_10_s3: Draw B3 to the module output (M3). Switch on.
exp_2_10_h1: Just like the blinking light – only with the buzzer.
exp_2_10_h2: The module output switches the path to 0V.
exp_2_10_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → B2, buzzer B2–B3, B3 → M3.
exp_2_10_erklaerung: The blinker module is like a button that presses and releases by itself. Whatever hangs on its output is switched in rhythm – a light blinks, a buzzer beeps.
exp_2_10_mehr: On the panel loudspeaker you can even see the pulses: its light ring blinks with every pulse.
exp_2_10_w1: Connect the panel loudspeaker (LS1/LS2) instead of the buzzer and watch the light ring.
exp_2_10_echt: Reversing beepers on lorries and alarm clocks beep in rhythm – there's a similar timing circuit behind them.
exp_2_11_frage: A traffic light for your bedroom door: with a changeover switch either red or green should light. Is that possible?
exp_2_11_v1: Yes, the changeover switch picks one of the two.
exp_2_11_b1: Depending on the position red or green lights, never both.
exp_2_11_s1: Put the changeover switch on A1–A3. Put the resistors from A1 to B1 and from A3 to B3 (vertical).
exp_2_11_s2: Put the red LED on B1–C1 and the green one on B3–C3, long leg at the top each.
exp_2_11_s3: Draw +9V to A2, C1 to 0V and C3 to C1. Switch to green.
exp_2_11_h1: Each LED needs its own series resistor.
exp_2_11_h2: The middle of the changeover switch gets +9V; A leads to red, B to green.
exp_2_11_loesung: W1 A1–A3, +9V → A2, R1 A1–B1, red LED B1–C1, R2 A3–B3, green LED B3–C3, C3 → C1 → 0V; switch to B (green).
exp_2_11_erklaerung: The changeover switch connects its middle to either one path or the other. That's why exactly one colour lights at a time: it chooses.
exp_2_11_mehr: Green LEDs need a bit more voltage than red ones, about 2.1 V instead of 1.9 V.
exp_2_11_w1: Add a yellow LED. Can you switch it on additionally with a push button?
exp_2_11_echt: Make a door traffic light out of paper: red means 'Do not disturb', green means 'Come in'.
exp_2_12_frage: You swap the 470 Ω resistor for a 1 kΩ one. Does the LED get brighter or dimmer?
exp_2_12_s1: Put a resistor on B3–B4 and set it to 1 kΩ (part menu: Value, or the toolbox).
exp_2_12_s2: Put the red LED on B4–C4, draw +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_12_h1: The colour bands for 1 kΩ are brown, black, red.
exp_2_12_h2: In the toolbox you can enter the value and apply it.
exp_2_12_loesung: 1 kΩ resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, +9V → B3, C4 → 0V.
exp_2_12_erklaerung: A bigger resistor slows the current down more. Less current flows through the LED and it shines less – but safely.
exp_2_12_mehr: With 1 kΩ about (9 V − 1.9 V) / 1000 Ω ≈ 7 mA flows instead of 15 mA.
exp_2_12_w1: Try 220 Ω, 470 Ω and 2.2 kΩ. Order them by brightness.
exp_2_12_echt: On many devices the power light is deliberately dim with a big resistor so it doesn't dazzle at night.
